newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Gallaher attacks advertising ban.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Gallaher attacks advertising ban.

text.p: Peter Wilson, chairman and chief executive of Gallaher, Britain's largest cigarette maker and owners of the Benson and Hedges and Silk Cut brands, on Friday attacked plans by the newly elected Labour Party to ban cigarette advertising.
"It will not have an effect on the overall consumption of cigarettes because that is not the effect of advertising," said Wilson in an interview.
On Wednesday Queen Elizabeth, in her speech opening the new parliament, said the government planned to publish a draft bill for an effective ban on advertising.

Labour Party officials said the White Paper would come out this summer and the party was determined to carry through its commitment to an ad ban during the current session of parliament, which will last until late 1998.
Tobacco executives point to the fact that tobacco consumption has actually risen in Norway since a ban on advertising was imposed.

Gallaher, which announced earlier its plan to list on the London stock market on May 30 following its demerger from American Brands Inc, will seek to expand overseas to combat declining sales in Britain, Wilson said.

"We will continue to develop our position in the U.K. market and equally on international expansion. The development of our international business is becoming increasingly important as the U.K. market declines," he said.
Gallaher will aim to build on sales elsewhere in Europe, Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, he said.
British cigarette sales are declining by 2.5 percent a year but within this sales of low tar cigarettes like Silk Cut have been growing.
Cut-price cigarettes are also taking a bigger share of the total as smokers are forced to step down to cheaper brands by progressive increases in tobacco duty imposed by government.
Former chancellor Kenneth Clarke promised to raise tobacco proces by inflation plus three percent a year.
The main threat in the future for Gallaher in Britain is not an ad ban but competition in brands, said Wilson.
"We have a strong presence in the premium sector built up over a long period of time and that brand equity will stand us in good stead."
Gallaher's competitor Imperial's premium brands, which include Embassy and Regal, are seen as weaker than Gallaher's but it has a stronger presence in the cut-price sector with Lambert & Butler.
Gallaher has responded by launching two new brands at the low price end -- Mayfair and Sovereign.

Gallaher and Imperial dominate Britain's 11.5 billion stg tobacco market. In cigarettes Gallaher has a 39.1 percent share and Imperial 37.8 percent while the combined share of its rivals Marlboro, Rothmans and Raffles is 23.1 percent.
Gallaher's Benson and Hedges and Silk Cut brands account for 14.3 percent of the 81.5 billion cigarettes sold in Britain in 1996. Silk cut is the best selling low-tar blend.
Wilson said the company expects a high level of interest in the group's shares from institutions in both America and Britain.
He declined to be drawn on a price for the stock when trading begins on May 30, but analysts said they expect the company to be valued at 2.2 billion pounds with a share price around 320p.
Some 95 percent of Gallaher shares will be held initially by American Brand shareholders but much of it is expected to flow back to British investors once trading begins.
